title: Observability for Data Pipelines
summary: Infra can be all green — CPU fine, latency fine, no errors in the logs — while a silent logic bug corrupts every row a pipeline writes. Data observability watches the data itself, continuously, not just the systems that move it.

slides.markdown:
[Quality checks](data-quality-fundamentals) run at specific points, on-demand or per-load. **Data observability** is the always-on version — continuous monitoring of every table in the pipeline for the signals that indicate something's wrong, so a problem surfaces automatically instead of waiting for the next scheduled check or a stakeholder complaint.

The core insight: infrastructure monitoring (CPU, memory, error logs) and data observability are answering genuinely different questions, and a pipeline can be perfectly healthy on the first while being badly broken on the second.

Data observability is usually organized around four signals, distinct from infrastructure metrics: **freshness** (did this table update when it was supposed to), **volume** (does the row count look normal, or has it spiked or dropped), **schema** (did the structure change unexpectedly — a column dropped, a type changed), and **distribution** (do the actual values look statistically normal — a percentage column suddenly full of values over 100, a category column that's 90% null when it's normally under 1%).

Each pillar catches a category of failure the others structurally can't — a table can be perfectly fresh and the right volume while its distribution has quietly gone haywire, and vice versa.

slides.sectionTitle: Monitors on every table, not just infra
slides.markdown:
Traditional infrastructure monitoring sits on servers, jobs, and queues. Data observability adds a second layer of monitors sitting directly on top of every table in the pipeline, watching the data's own behavior independent of whether the infrastructure underneath looks healthy.

![Infra monitoring and data observability as two independent layers over the same pipeline](assets/two-monitoring-layers.svg)

assets.alt: Infra monitoring and data observability as two independent layers over the same pipeline

slides.markdown:
**Freshness monitoring** tracks `MAX(updated_at)` (or an equivalent watermark) on a table against its expected update cadence, and alerts when the gap exceeds what's normal — a table that updates hourly but hasn't updated in four hours is stale, even though nothing about the table's schema or row count looks wrong.

The subtlety worth getting right: "expected cadence" often isn't a flat number. A table that only updates on business days will show a real, harmless gap every weekend — a freshness monitor that doesn't account for that pattern either misses real staleness during the week (because the threshold was set loose enough to tolerate weekends) or cries wolf every single weekend (because it wasn't). Getting the expected-cadence model right, including its legitimate quiet periods, is most of the actual work.

**Volume anomaly detection** compares a table's row count on each load against a learned normal range — usually a rolling baseline that accounts for day-of-week or seasonal patterns, not a single fixed number — and flags loads that fall well outside it in either direction.

Both directions matter and mean different things: a sudden *drop* usually points at an upstream data-loss problem (a source stopped sending, a filter condition broke); a sudden *spike* can mean a genuine business event (a viral campaign, a real traffic surge) or a pipeline bug (a join that started fanning out duplicate rows). The alert looks identical either way — a number outside the expected band — so volume anomaly detection tells you *something* changed, and a human still has to figure out which of the very different explanations actually applies.

| | Infra observability | Data observability |
|---|---|---|
| What it watches | Servers, jobs, queues — CPU, memory, latency, error logs, queue depth | The data itself — freshness, volume, schema, distribution of actual table contents |
| Catches | The pipeline crashed, ran out of resources, or is running slowly | The pipeline ran fine but produced data that's stale, incomplete, or statistically wrong |
| A green infra dashboard implies | The systems moving data are healthy | Nothing about whether the data itself is correct |

The two are complementary, not competing — a mature pipeline needs both, because each one is structurally blind to the failures the other one catches.

A job completes on schedule, CPU and memory usage are unremarkable, no errors in any log — every infra dashboard shows green. Meanwhile, a logic bug introduced in the last deploy silently corrupts a calculation on every single row: a currency conversion applied twice, a join condition that duplicates every row with more than one match, a date filter with an off-by-one that drops the most recent day every time.

None of these produce an error. The job succeeds by every infrastructure metric that exists, because infrastructure monitoring was never designed to check whether the *content* of the output is correct — only whether the systems that produced it behaved normally. This is precisely the gap data observability exists to close, and it's why "all our monitoring is green" is not the same claim as "our data is correct," no matter how comprehensive the infra monitoring is.

A typical observability tool's monitor definition, conceptually similar across most modern platforms:

```yaml
monitor: fct_orders_freshness
table: fct_orders
metric: max(updated_at)
expected_cadence: hourly
business_hours_only: false
alert:
  channel: pagerduty
  severity: high
  threshold: "gap > 3 hours"

monitor: fct_orders_volume
table: fct_orders
metric: row_count
baseline: rolling_7day_same_weekday
alert:
  channel: slack
  severity: medium
  threshold: "deviation > 40% from baseline"
```

Both monitors run automatically on a schedule, without anyone needing to remember to check the table manually — which is the entire point of observability over manual, periodic quality checks: it's continuous and doesn't depend on someone happening to look at the right moment.

A monitor that fires into a channel nobody watches is functionally the same as no monitor at all. Alert routing — which team, which specific person, which paging tool a given monitor's failure reaches — has to be decided deliberately, tied back to the [ownership metadata](data-catalogs-metadata) a catalog should already be tracking for that table.

The common failure: a monitor gets set up during an incident postmortem, routed to whoever happened to be debugging that incident, and six months later that person has moved teams and nobody else knows the alert exists or what it means when it fires. Alert ownership needs the same ongoing-maintenance discipline as everything else in this group — assigned deliberately, tied to a real team, and reviewed periodically rather than set once during a fire and forgotten.

slides.sectionTitle: Closing the loop back into contracts and quality
slides.markdown:
Observability findings shouldn't just resolve an incident and disappear — the strongest teams feed them back into the mechanisms earlier in this group. A volume anomaly traced to an upstream schema change that a [contract](data-contracts) didn't cover becomes a reason to extend that contract's SLA or semantics coverage. A distribution anomaly that revealed a business logic assumption nobody had written down becomes a new quality check, so the same failure is caught automatically next time instead of needing another manual investigation.

This is the actual throughline of the whole group: quality, contracts, lineage, catalogs, access control, and observability aren't six separate practices — they're one continuous discipline of turning implicit assumptions into explicit, enforced, and continuously-checked ones, each feeding the others as gaps get discovered.

A junior answer to "how do you know your pipelines are healthy" points at a green infrastructure dashboard. A senior answer distinguishes the two questions explicitly — is the system that moves data healthy, and is the data it produced actually correct — and can describe monitors for at least freshness and volume as the baseline, with alert ownership tied to a real, current team rather than whoever happened to be on call the day it was configured.

That distinction — infra health is not data health — is the single idea worth carrying out of this entire group into any pipeline you build or inherit.
